analysis.one_liner: Replaces federal income taxes with a 20% flat tax on wages and businesses, and caps federal spending.
analysis.headline: The flat tax bill never got a vote: introduced in June 1994 with 16 Republican cosponsors, it died in committee when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would replace today's individual and corporate income taxes with a single flat rate of 20 percent, dropping to 17 percent after two years, applied only to earned wages and active business income, not to investment returns at the individual level. It would raise the standard deduction sharply, end automatic tax withholding from paychecks, and wipe out itemized deductions like mortgage interest. It would also cap growth in entitlement spending (with automatic cuts if exceeded), require a balanced budget by 2000, and require the government to compensate property owners when agency actions reduce property value by 10 percent or more.
analysis.who_benefits: The largest gains go to corporations and households with substantial investment income: the corporate rate would drop from a top of 35 percent to 20 percent (then 17), and investment returns would no longer be taxed at the individual level at all. Higher earners also gain from the single low rate. Working families with modest wages benefit from the very large standard deduction — a joint filer could earn $24,700 plus $5,000 per dependent before owing anything — and everyone gains from simpler filing.

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the graduated individual income tax with a flat 20 percent rate (17 percent after 1996) on earned income above a standard deduction of $24,700 for joint filers, $16,200 for heads of household, and $12,350 for singles, plus $5,000 per dependent [S3].
Replaces the corporate tax with a flat 20 percent (later 17 percent) tax on active business income, payable by every person engaged in a business, not just corporations [S3].
Ends income tax withholding from wages after 1994, so workers would receive their full paycheck and pay tax themselves [S3].

Caps growth in total entitlement and mandatory spending (excluding Social Security) at inflation plus eligible-population growth from 1995 through 2000, enforced by automatic across-the-board cuts, and sets maximum total spending levels through 1999 as a path to a balanced budget by 2000 [S3].

Requires federal agencies to compensate private property owners when a final agency action measurably reduces property value, treating a 10 percent or larger loss as eligible, with the agency required to stay the action while making an offer [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Because only earned income is taxed at the individual level, the tax burden shifts toward wages and away from investment returns; workers earning above the deduction bear income tax while capital gains, dividends, and interest do not. Federal benefit recipients — including Medicare patients, retirees, veterans, and low-income households — face automatic payment cuts whenever entitlement spending grows faster than the capped rate. Taxpayers also bear the cost of compensating property owners whose land value drops from agency decisions, and workers take on the burden of estimating and paying their own taxes without withholding.

drawbacks.text: The individual tax applies only to earned income, so interest, dividends, and capital gains would go untaxed at the personal level; households whose income comes mainly from investments would owe little or nothing, while wage earners above the deduction would pay the full rate [S3].

The entitlement caps are enforced by automatic sequestration: Medicare payments could be cut up to 4 percent, federal retirement and veterans' benefits up to 2 percent, and low-income programs like food stamps, Medicaid, and AFDC up to 1 percent, with cuts repeating in later years [S3].
The bill replaces all current individual tax procedures with the standard deduction, eliminating itemized deductions including mortgage interest and the deduction for state and local taxes [S2, S3].

Repealing withholding would end automatic tax collection from paychecks, leaving each worker responsible for estimating and paying tax on their own — a mechanism that historically has made collection harder and shifted the compliance burden onto individuals [S3].

The property compensation requirement would obligate taxpayers to pay owners whenever any final agency action measurably cuts land value by 10 percent or more, which could make routine environmental, zoning, and land-use enforcement substantially more expensive for the public [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's simplification and its zero-tax floor for low-wage families are real, substantial benefits, and a balanced-budget process has genuine appeal. But the design is heavily weighted toward those with capital: cutting the top rates for businesses and high earners while exempting investment income from personal tax produces its largest gains at the top, and it offsets those revenue losses with automatic, ongoing cuts to Medicare, retirement, veterans' and low-income benefits. Repealing withholding also transfers collection work from employers to workers. An honest assessment: a simpler tax code was achievable without simultaneously narrowing the tax base away from investment income and hardwiring benefit cuts.

outcome.mechanism: Armey introduced the bill in June 1994 and it was referred to three committees, but no committee acted on it and it never reached the House floor before the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Rep. Richard Armey introduced the bill on June 16, 1994 [S1, S5].
It was referred jointly on the same day to the House Committees on Ways and Means, Government Operations, and Rules [S5].
On June 21, 1994, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Legislation and National Security of Government Operations — the last recorded action in its history [S5].
No markup, hearing, or floor vote is recorded before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Everyone whose finances depended on the existing tax code kept it: homeowners with mortgage interest deductions, investors whose returns were taxed under the existing schedule, and recipients of Medicare, veterans', retirement, and low-income benefits avoided the bill's automatic spending cuts.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 sponsors and cosponsors were House Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and no vote was ever taken that could have tested bipartisan support [S4].

industries.note: The bill replaces the graduated corporate tax (top rate 35 percent at the time) with a flat 20 percent, falling to 17 percent, on active business income. The revenue loss is not offset in the bill, so the burden falls on other taxpayers or federal services. [S3]

Individual tax applies only to earned income, so interest, dividends, and capital gains would be untaxed at the personal level, and the single low rate replaces the then-current top individual rate of 39.6 percent. The largest dollar savings go to those with the most capital income. [S3]

Replacing itemized deductions with a standard deduction eliminates the mortgage interest deduction, removing a subsidy that has boosted home purchase borrowing — a loss for the industry, though the deduction itself costs the treasury. [S2, S3]

A flat tax with no itemized deductions would sharply shrink demand for tax preparation, but repealing withholding would create new filing and payment chores for every worker, partly offsetting that loss. [S3]
Owners become entitled to taxpayer-funded compensation whenever an agency action cuts property value by 10 percent or more, converting regulatory disputes into claims against the treasury. [S3]
